title: Tier IV Checkpoint II — A Grounded, Critical View

pts: Universal Grammar's accessibility to adult learners and the Critical Period Hypothesis's exact shape both remain genuinely open scholarly questions.
Neither uncertainty should produce discouragement — adult learners demonstrably achieve high, genuinely functional proficiency regardless.
Accurate, honest representation of this uncertainty serves learners better than false theoretical or practical certainty.

v: Learner questions on cards (written for this book)

items: Read three questions learners and parents often ask about age and language learning.
In pairs, draft an answer that is honest about what research knows and does not know (Units 86–87).
Remove any false certainty, in either direction.
Add one practical suggestion that helps the learner whatever the theory.
Share and refine answers as a group.
Role-play a parent meeting where the answers are used.
Support: provide a model answer for the first question.
Challenge: cite one study in plain language in each answer.

blocks.x: A question and two answers (written for this book):

lines: Question: I am 35. Is it too late for me to speak English well?
Overconfident answer: Adults can learn exactly like children if they work hard.

Honest answer: Researchers still debate how age affects language learning. Adults who start late rarely sound exactly like people who grew up with English, but many reach high, fully useful levels. What makes most difference now is how much English you hear, read and use. Let’s plan that together.

blocks.x: Honest uncertainty respects learners more than either discouragement or false promises.

points.h: Bilingualism's Benefits Are Real But More Modest Than Popular Belief
pts: Genuine executive-function and metalinguistic benefits exist, but popular claims of broad cognitive enhancement overstate the careful evidence.
This connects to Unit 73's ethics-and-validity work — honest representation of evidence remains a genuine professional obligation.
Bilingualism's real value doesn't require inflated claims to justify continued strong support for multilingual education.

lines: Bilingual children are more aware of how language works. → fairly well supported.
Bilingualism gives better control of attention. → disputed; findings are mixed.
Learning two languages makes you more intelligent. → overstated.
A: If the attention advantage is disputed, why support bilingual education?
B: Because children learn best when they understand the language of instruction, and because their languages matter for family, identity and community.

body: In a famous study of adults who had learned Spanish at school, much vocabulary was lost in the first few years, but what remained was often retained for decades (Bahrick 1984). How well something is learned in the first place affects how long it lasts.

points.h: Maintenance Deserves as Much Attention as Acquisition
pts: Language skills, once built, require ongoing maintenance strategy or genuinely risk attrition over time.
This connects to Unit 56's advanced-autonomy work — sustained self-directed practice matters well beyond any course's formal end.
Course design should explicitly plan for this full arc, not just initial acquisition within a bounded course period.

v: A course outline; maintenance planning sheet

items: Identify what learners will need to keep after the course ends: vocabulary, reading fluency, speaking confidence.
With learners, list realistic maintenance activities: reading, listening, conversation clubs, apps, writing.
Each learner writes a maintenance plan for six months, with weekly targets.
Build a final lesson where learners share plans and form support pairs.
Arrange a check-in, for example by message, after three months.
For teachers, create a personal English-maintenance plan, especially for those working in schools where English is rarely used.
Support: provide a menu of activities with time estimates.
Challenge: learners design a learning contract (Unit 56).

Every month: write one blog post; check my vocabulary notebook.

aims.x: This checkpoint pauses before the final stretch of the book. Units 86–94 moved from acquisition theory to the systems within which English teaching happens: teacher education, research publishing, international testing, educational technology and the world’s wider linguistic ecology. The unit draws these threads together into one grounded, critical view. Each point revisits one unit, asks what we can honestly claim from the evidence, and turns that claim into a practical task for teachers or teacher educators.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: represent open questions in acquisition theory honestly to learners and colleagues;
state the benefits of bilingualism accurately, without overstatement;
plan for language maintenance as well as acquisition in course design;
evaluate teacher-development programmes against research evidence;
identify one realistic way to contribute to the field’s knowledge;
advise learners on high-stakes exams with informed judgement;
evaluate technology claims with the same rigour as any research claim;
place English teaching within the wider multilingual world.

why: Why this matters. Checkpoint I connected core theory to practice. This checkpoint connects that theory to the wider institutional and global systems ELT actually operates within.

background.x: Part IV has repeatedly met the same pattern: a popular certainty that the research does not quite support. It is widely believed that adults cannot learn a language well, that bilingualism makes children cleverer, that technology transforms learning and that high exam scores prove real-world ability. In each case the careful evidence is more interesting: real effects, real limits and open questions. Unit 81 gave the tools to read such evidence; this unit uses them across nine topics at once.

The acquisition debates remain open. Researchers still disagree about whether Universal Grammar remains accessible to adult learners (White 2003), and a very large online study suggested that the ability to learn grammar declines only in late adolescence, while also showing that later learners can reach high proficiency (Hartshorne, Tenenbaum and Pinker 2018). Reviews stress that age effects are tangled with the amount and quality of input, motivation and schooling (Muñoz and Singleton 2011). Research on bilingual cognitive advantages is similarly contested (Bialystok, Craik and Luk 2012; Paap and Greenberg 2013). Research on memory for school-learned languages shows both loss and remarkable long-term retention (Bahrick 1984).

For teacher education the picture also has nuance. Mary Kennedy’s (2016) review found that what professional development asks teachers to do, and how it helps them act on ideas in their own classrooms, matters more than the number of hours. NEP 2020 expects teachers to take part in at least 50 hours of continuous professional development each year (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020) [VERIFY paragraph]; Units 90 and 68 suggest how those hours can be spent well. The final stretch of the book, Units 96–100, takes the critical awareness of Unit 59 further, into native-speakerism, linguistic rights, decolonizing ELT and the ethics of AI assessment.

terms.def: The loss or decline of language skills over time, usually because a language is no longer used regularly; it can affect a first language as well as a second.

The claim that using two languages improves executive functions such as attention control (Bialystok 2001); later studies found inconsistent results (Paap and Greenberg 2013), so the claim is now contested.
The hypothesis that there is a limited period in life during which a language can be acquired to native-like levels (Lenneberg 1967); its application to second languages is debated.

Teaching in which research evidence is one input, weighed alongside professional judgement, learners’ needs and local context. The term is often preferred to ‘evidence-based’ because it gives teachers a stronger role.
Keeping a language alive and in use, whether a community keeping its language despite pressure to shift, or an individual keeping proficiency after formal study ends.

The relationships between languages and their speakers within a society and its environment (Haugen 1972); the term draws attention to how one language’s growth, such as English, can affect the health of others.

The ability to reflect on language as an object, noticing and talking about its forms and rules; multilingual learners often show this ability strongly, comparing structures across Kannada, Hindi and English.
Teacher development that takes place within daily teaching, such as through lesson study, peer observation or classroom inquiry, rather than in one-off workshops.

Deciding what a test score does and does not show about a learner’s ability. A high exam score may not prove real-world performance, so scores must be read in the light of what the test actually measured.
Chomsky’s proposal that humans have innate principles common to all languages, which constrain and guide language acquisition (Chomsky 1965). Its role in second language learning remains debated.
